articles.title: CONCACAF asks Infantino to skip youth event amid FIFA governance crisis
articles.excerpt: CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani has asked FIFA chief Gianni Infantino to ⁠stay away from a youth football tournament in the Dominican Republic this weekend, saying his presence would overshadow ...
articles.body_text:
CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani has asked FIFA chief Gianni Infantino to ⁠stay away from a youth football tournament in the Dominican Republic this weekend, saying his presence would overshadow the event due to mounting opposition to his leadership.

Infantino ⁠is under pressure from three confederations to resign, including Europe’s UEFA, Asia’s AFC and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean, after his aborted proposal to sell a stake in the World Cup.

Infantino, who could potentially face a vote of no confidence ‌from world football’s regional powerhouses, is visiting the Dominican Republic this weekend and was reportedly planning to attend a competition organised by the Caribbean Football Union (CFU).

In a letter sent to Infantino on Friday and seen by the Reuters news agency, Montagliani cited the “governance crisis surrounding FIFA” as the reason for the FIFA president to reconsider attending the CFU U-14 Series event.

“As you may be aware, your proposed attendance has garnered significant media ⁠attention,” Montagliani, who is also a vice president on the FIFA Council, ⁠wrote.

“…the media will focus on this situation, which will unfortunately significantly take away from the technical nature of the CFU youth competition.

“As such, I respectfully ask you in the name of football to reconsider your ⁠attendance as it will unfortunately undermine the technical nature of this important youth development activity.”

Al Jazeera Sport has contacted FIFA for comment.

Infantino was ⁠received at Punta Cana by the Dominican Republic’s Minister ⁠of Sports and Recreation Kelvin Cruz.

“We deeply appreciate your visit to the Dominican Republic, without doubt that your presence in our country puts us on the international football radar and opens us great prospects for growth and ‌development of Dominican football,” Cruz said in a statement.

Infantino was also welcomed by Dominican Football Federation President Jose Deschamps, National Commissioner of Football Benny Metz and Olympic Committee President ‌Garibaldy ‌Bautista Lorenzo.

Infantino is seeking a fourth term until 2031, but several national associations and key officials have withdrawn support for the Swiss administrator.

articles.title: Jets say Geno Smith delivers 'exactly what we were looking for' in 2026 debut, so here comes the overreaction
articles.excerpt:
Former New York Jets quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick believes Geno Smith, as well as linebacker Demario Davis, will provide leadership qualities and more in their New York reunion.

Geno Smith played wel...
articles.body_text:
Former New York Jets quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick believes Geno Smith, as well as linebacker Demario Davis, will provide leadership qualities and more in their New York reunion.

Geno Smith played well in his New York Jets debut on Friday night and in any other town, that's going to be notable but somewhat mundane news because the starting quarterback performing at a high level in the preseason is not a promise of championships.

But because we're talking about New York, and the starving-for-glad-tidings Jets, this space warns you to prepare for what's next.

Because Smith's one drive against the Pittsburgh Steelers might lead to some massive overreaction. And a lot of excitement. And high expectations.

JETS FANS BREATHE SIGH OF RELIEF AFTER PRACTICE SCARE FOR $43M STAR RUNNING BACK

New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith greets teammates before an NFL preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, in Pittsburgh. (AP Photo/Justin Berl)

So, the Geno 2.0 public relations uproar is on.

That's how it is in the Big Apple's thrill ride through the NFL season for quarterbacks who struggle in preseason practices, as Smith has done at times this summer, and then deliver a near-perfect performance in their first preseason action.

"Very, very efficient," Jets coach Aaron Glenn described it to reporters afterward. "I mean, I think he had two third-down completions within that, threw to five different receivers within that drive. He looked very comfortable.

"It was exactly what we were looking for ..."

Smith is thus going to get a good dose of New York pundit love for the next few days because he had that drive in which he completed all seven of his pass attempts, including one that was tipped and caught by one of his offensive linemen.

He's going to get applauded for converting a couple of third-down situations. And, of course, the 13-yard touchdown pass to Jelani Woods will be replayed as if on a loop on channels 2, 4, 5, 7 and WPIX.

New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith throws during the first half of an NFL preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, in Pittsburgh. (AP Photo/Gene J. Puskar)

"It felt good to be out there with the guys," Smith told reporters gathered at his locker stall. "You know, obviously we got one drive in, but we scored a touchdown. You always want to start fast. so that was a good thing.

"But definitely a lot of room for improvement. So just looking forward to getting back to practice, getting to work."

This is a perfect reaction from Smith. He shows modesty while giving his performance proper context.

But the fans? The media? They're going to go as close to wild as is allowed by NFL preseason bylaws.

And it won't be just the fans and media getting all pumped. Some Jets teammates will, too.

IT'S WISE NOT TO TRUST THE NFL PRESEASON BUT, HOLY MOLY, RAMS QB TY SIMPSON LOOKS LIKE A STUD

"We were all fired up for him," backup quarterback Cade Klubnik said. "He's going to have a heck of a year and that's just a glimpse of it."

There it is, a prediction for the entire regular season based on one preseason drive.

Geno Smith of the New York Jets participates in a joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Atlantic Health Jets Training Center in Florham Park, N.J., on Aug. 11, 2026. (Getty Images)

And, again, it was a good drive. But that Steelers defense that retreated did not include T.J. Watt, or Jalen Ramsey, or Joey Porter, or Cam Heyward.

Look, the Smith we saw on Friday was more comfortable, more proficient, and just better than the one who left this same franchise a decade ago as a draft bust.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

You'll recall Smith's first stint with the Jets, from 2013 to 2016, was a mess. It ended, for all intents and purposes, when teammate IK Enemkpali sucker punched Smith and broke his jaw in 2015.

That, unfortunately, turned Smith's stint with the team into something of a punchline — literally.

So, this return has a wonderful opportunity to be something else. Something better.

But Friday's lone drive should be understood to be one humble hint of that possibility rather than a bold vision of the next few months.

"I just feel like," he said, "we can be a lot better."

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

articles.title: The Berlin Wall separated his family. Its legacy still endures
articles.excerpt:
This feature is the first in a series examining how artificial borders reshape daily life, divide families and force loved ones to navigate the human cost of political geography.

Erich Guetinger was ...
articles.body_text:
This feature is the first in a series examining how artificial borders reshape daily life, divide families and force loved ones to navigate the human cost of political geography.

Erich Guetinger was 18 years old when he first saw his uncle’s family as an adult.

Having last seen them as a small child, Guetinger was both excited and nervous to see his uncle, aunt, and two older cousins after so long.

It was the summer of 1969 – the Beatles were recording Abbey Road, the United States had begun withdrawing troops from Vietnam, and Neil Armstrong was about to become the first person to walk on the moon.

By then, Germany had been divided for two decades. The Federal Republic of Germany, or West Germany, was a capitalist democracy aligned with the US and Western Europe. The German Democratic Republic, or East Germany, was a Soviet-aligned socialist state governed by the Socialist Unity Party. Berlin itself had been divided since 1945, and the construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961 had hardened that separation.

The two states differed sharply in size and population. About 51 million people lived in West Germany and about 18 million in East Germany, separated by a nearly 2,000km (1,242 miles) border running from the Baltic Sea to the Czechoslovak border. By 1969, West Germany’s population had grown to about 61 million, while East Germany’s had fallen to roughly 17 million.

With most of his family in their hometown of Babenhausen, Bavaria, and his uncle Hans, aunt Frieda, and cousins Dieter and Guenter in Brieskow-Finkenheerd, a village near Frankfurt an der Oder in East Germany, the Guetingers were directly affected by Germany’s political partition.

A journey that would take just a few hours by car was, back then, a trip requiring visa approval, designated transit corridors, and border guard inspections.

It was the lengths they had to go through that had caused the young Guetinger some unease.

“My dad and I set off for our trip on a Saturday afternoon,” recalled Guetinger, a genial 75-year-old historian, author, and grandfather, who today lives in what would have been West Berlin.

“After a visa process lasting two to three weeks, during which we had to inform GDR officials where we were staying and the purpose of the trip, we set off for one of the three transit corridors that served as official points of entry and exit between the two countries,” he explained.

They travelled by train through a Bavarian border crossing into Probstzella, in the GDR.

“As soon as the train entered GDR territory”, Guetinger said, “we were stopped, and border guards checked our visas and IDs".

The pair stayed in Frankfurt an der Oder for a week, meeting the family’s friends, eating fresh meat and spending quality time at the small family home.

“My uncle was keen to introduce his brother from the West to all his friends,” Guetinger recounts with a smile.

“It was a nice trip, and while we hadn’t seen each other in some time, we got along well.”

They returned home to Bavaria just in time to see Armstrong take his first step on the moon, which they watched with Guetinger’s other uncle, Erich, and some of his friends.

“Even now, I vividly remember the blurred black-and-white pictures appearing on TV. The distance between us wasn’t very far, but making that trip from Bavaria to Frankfurt an der Oder seemed as far as going to the moon and back.”

At least two generations on both Guetinger’s maternal and paternal sides were from Babenhausen, a small Bavarian market town of about 4,000 people in the 1960s. Surrounded by a castle, it was once home to a merchant family said to have been prominent during the Middle Ages.

Guetinger’s father, Ernst, was among five siblings and the youngest of the three boys. Hans was the eldest, followed by another brother, Erich, and there was a four-year age gap between Ernst and Hans. Guetinger said this age difference played a role in his father's and uncle's relationship.

“My dad and uncle Hans didn’t have a very close relationship because they had grown up during wartime,” he said. “When war broke out in 1939, Uncle Hans was obliged to serve as a soldier.”

Soldiers were in short supply, so German boys aged 16 and 17 were drafted as “Flakhelfer” to work with anti-aircraft guns or man the huge lights that tracked enemy aircraft.

“My Uncle Erich was in this age range so served in this role, but my dad, being the youngest, did not have to serve,” he added.

After Nazi Germany’s defeat in 1945, the country was divided into occupation zones and then formally split into two separate countries in 1949.

Hans returned to Babenhausen, Bavaria, after the war and looked for work as a shoemaker. But jobs were scarce, and he had trouble finding work.

Amid their struggles, Hans’s homesick wife encouraged him to try finding work in the GDR, where she was from. They knew they would be welcomed, because the GDR was keen on people willing to buck the trend of those going west - roughly 2.7 million people moved to West Germany between 1949 and 1961 – for better economic and employment opportunities.

In 1958, Hans's family moved east to Brieskow-Finkenheerd, a village near the Polish border, where Hans started working at a power station that also provided their accommodation. He was also able to indulge in his love of hunting as much as he liked.

“He was very happy hunting,” Guetinger remembered fondly. “In West Germany, you could only hunt if you owned land, but since the government owned all the land in the GDR, my uncle was told he could hunt wherever he wanted.”

Hans became so well known for his hunting abilities that when the big cadres wanted to celebrate something and eat some tasty meat like boar or wild swine, they would ask Hans to go hunting.

“The party had its own hunters, but they considered my uncle one of the best,” Guetinger said.

Meanwhile, Hans’s younger brother Ernst, back in Bavaria, became a father to Erich Guetinger in 1951.

In the 1950s, freedom of movement between the two countries remained largely unrestricted, but from the 1960s onwards, tougher measures were instituted. After that, East Germans were generally only allowed to travel to the West for urgent family matters, such as funerals or weddings.

In August 1961 – 65 years ago – the East German government began building the Berlin Wall, a 155km (96 miles) concrete structure surrounding West Berlin that effectively isolated it within GDR territory and severed the capital.

Outside Berlin, efforts to fortify the division led to the installation of new barbed wire fences, detectors, watchtowers, as well as booby-traps and extended powers for border guards to shoot and arrest escapees. Between then and 1989, when the wall came down, an estimated 75,000 people were imprisoned for trying to escape.

Guetinger says that in the early years of the division, there was barely any contact with his uncle and family.

“Eventually, we were able to start sending letters, but we shared very little in these because everybody knew the East German secret police, known as the Stasi, would carefully check the post between families, often reading our letters,” he said.

Like many families in West Germany, the Guetingers would often send Western products to their relatives in the East.

“For Christmas, we made parcels containing things we knew they would like, and which we knew it would be difficult for them to get, such as coffee and blue jeans," Guetinger said.

"Blue jeans were particularly hot property, and my cousins liked this kind of clothing. And even though we would send parcels, there was always a chance that they wouldn’t reach them,” he explained, noting that shipments were closely monitored.

Guetinger says it is still hard to fully assess how the day-to-day disruption caused by the division impacted their family’s sense of safety and unity.

“Even if my parents had a heavy heart back then, they would rarely talk about it, so today, I have to rely on other indicators to try and understand. And one of the indicators is that my dad and his elder brother tried to visit each other as soon as it was possible for both of them.”

Yet, even with the 1969 trip being made possible, Guetinger paints a picture of an uneasy time clouded by the fear of Stasi spies.

“We have been sitting here for more than 30 minutes and not once have I looked over my shoulder,” he said. “I’m not afraid of saying something private or political. I don’t care if anyone is listening.”

“During that trip, as soon as we entered anywhere, we first had to scan the room to see who was there and how far they were away from us," he said, noting how this determined their topics of conversation.

"Uncle Hans had a lot of friends whom he met regularly outside of his house, and they did this every time they met. It was understood that the secret service was everywhere, and they could make life very difficult for you.”

In 1973, Guetinger travelled to meet his friend in Hessen, West Germany, a trip that would see his life take an unexpected turn.

“My friend had a Chinese girlfriend called Hui-Chui Ma, and the plan was that she and her best friend would be joining us upon their return from a trip to Vienna. Her friend, Yan-Yun, was a nurse from China working in Freiburg, around 400km [250 miles] away from Hessen,” he explained.

“When we left, we got the train together, and eventually we went in different directions. But something had hit [Yan-Yun and I] like a lightning bolt.”

Germany’s division had also shaped family stories beyond its borders, with migration patterns evolving on either side depending on the political alignments and economic needs of each nation.

Alignment with countries inside the neighbouring Eastern Bloc, such as Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria, brought links with socially aligned nations on a global level. This led to approximately 70,000 contract workers from Vietnam, more than 20,000 young people from Mozambique, and a small number of engineers from North Korea coming to East Germany during the division. After unification, many of these migrant workers sought to stay on and build families.

West Germany, meanwhile, had friendly links with South Korea, Indonesia and Japan, among others.

Guetinger says that Yan-Yun came to West Germany through a recruitment drive for nurses initiated in Taiwan in the early 1970s.

The pair started to get to know each other, and despite the language barrier, they found that they had something in common.

“The Chiang family shared a common experience... their extended family had been split by the political tensions between mainland China and Taiwan,” he explained.

“Yan-Yun was born in what was then Peking [Beijing today], and at the age of two, her family fled to Taiwan, where she stayed until she came to West Germany. But they had no idea if other family members in mainland China had survived the internal war.”

The relationship between the couple developed quickly, and in the summer of 1974, Guetinger moved with Yan-Yun to West Berlin, where he began studying Chinese politics at the Free University. Like many West Berliners, he took advantage of having better freedom of movement, including the ability to travel to and from the GDR.

“For me, as a student, it was interesting to go to East Berlin because the books there were much cheaper, plus the music in East Germany was very good, and you could get cheaper music discs.”

Yet, there were travel rules that West Germans had to obey, such as registering with local police on arrival. They also could not exchange East German Marks back into hard West German Deutsche Marks when leaving. Instead, they were required to deposit the money into an East German bank.

At the end of one trip, Guetinger went to deposit the money but encountered a long queue.

“So I decided to skip the deposit and placed the money in a pouch with my keys,” he said. “We had different currencies, and GDR money was of no value across the border, so it remained there for many months until I went back.”

On his next trip to East Berlin, the casually dressed student watched as border guards sitting at high counters let in West Germans who were carrying big, heavy bags. Travelling empty-handed, he thought his passage would be hassle-free.

But when the border police got to him, they stopped and ordered him to follow them. They took him to a very small room with no window and a neon light, and they asked him to remove everything from his pockets.

“One by one, out came my passport, some money and the pouch. ‘What’s that?’ the guard asked, and I told him it was for my keys. For a few seconds, I hoped that would be enough," he said.

"Then he ordered me to open it, and instead of finding a key, he found GDR money. This was a major offence, what they called ‘offending the rules concerning the transfer of money’.”

Guetinger was questioned about the purpose of his visit and then left alone for what he says was about 90 minutes while the guards decided his fate.

“I sat in that room alone, and I knew I was in some kind of trouble,” he recalled.

Guetinger says he was ultimately allowed to go because the guards were satisfied with who he was meeting – a well-known writer named Jan Koplowitz, a former member of the German Communist Party.

“I could leave because I had an appointment with this particular connection,” he said.

Guetinger later concluded that X-rays had been used at the border, and that was how the guards had established that he was carrying cash into the GDR.

“We didn’t know about this back then,” he added.

Despite the division, Guetinger’s family would find ways to meet, and sometimes broke rules to do so.

He recalls one such trip in the mid-1970s when his father came to visit him in West Berlin.

Guetinger says they decided to visit East Berlin and, at the last minute, decided to go on to visit his family in Frankfurt an der Oder.

Since the plan was hatched late in the day, it meant circumventing strict visa rules. A visa for East Berlin – which is all they had – meant they were only permitted to visit East Berlin and nowhere else in the GDR.

Guetinger says the trip quickly turned into a clandestine affair that involved coordination with his cousin and uncle. In East Germany, hardly anyone had a home phone, so they had to rely on public telephones or phones at work.

That constraint helped shape the family’s plan.

“My uncle and his son both worked at the power station, and anyone entering or leaving the power station had to report to the gatekeeper, who had a telephone. The gatekeeper liked eating fresh game, so in exchange for using the phone, my uncle would bring him deer or birds that he had hunted,” he said.

His cousin used the phone to speak with Guetinger and make the arrangements. Then, once in East Berlin, Guetinger and his family took the train as far as Karlshorst, a station about 30 minutes outside the city, where his cousin collected them by car.

“It was easier in a private car as we had less chance of being stopped by border guards than if we were on a train,” he said.

While it would have been possible to arrange to meet the family in East Berlin, they were eager to see where and how their family lived in the GDR. But they knew it was risky.

“If we had been caught, it would have been a problem not only for us but also for our family [in the East], as it would have been seen as a serious offence. We felt a genuine fear, but luckily, we were able to go and return without any trouble.”

West Germany established diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China in 1972. For Yan-Yun’s family, the new connection between West Berlin, Taiwan and mainland China created a possible channel for renewing contact.

Guetinger said the family used West Berlin as an informal postal hub, passing letters between relatives in Taiwan and relatives in mainland China.

“The reconnection with my wife’s relatives was managed by postal communication, where our family in Taiwan sent us letters to West Berlin, and we could send them on to addresses in China, and vice versa,” Guetinger explained. “We had the names and old addresses, and that was enough.”

In 1988, Guetinger and his wife – they had married in 1977 – were able to visit mainland China, marking Yan-Yun’s first time back in more than four decades.

“It was an important trip,” Guetinger said, noting that they visited his wife’s family home and her birthplace.

“Some years later, we met Yan-Yun’s mother in Taiwan and travelled together with her from Taiwan to the Chinese mainland to meet other family members in Kunming and Nanjing. The family had been apart for 40 years, and reconnecting with them had all started from West Berlin,” he explained.

Following months of mounting public pressure, the Berlin Wall finally fell on a cold November night in 1989. Guetinger says it was a “surreal” moment – and his family quickly started seeing one another again.

“By then, Uncle Hans had retired, and both he, my aunt and Guenter visited us a few times in West Berlin. My other cousin, however, didn’t come to visit. He was happy to stay in the countryside. From what I can recall, Uncle Hans never got to return to our hometown of Bavaria before he passed away,” he said.

Today, Guetinger remains in contact with his family from the former GDR, and both of his children have met that part of their family, with the sides visiting each other’s respective homes.

Similarly, the family is also close with their wider family in Taiwan and visits often. Guetinger, who in the early 2000s authored Die Geschichte der Chinesen in Deutschland (The History of the Chinese in Germany), and his wife were there again this summer.

German unification continues to be heralded as a celebration – a peaceful revolution for the people, by the people – but there remain strong signs that the seeds of separation sown during the division have in many ways taken root.

For many, the experience of unification was characterised by economic instability, with job losses and the privatisation of East German companies. While less extreme today, economic disparities between the regions persist.

Unification effectively saw the capitalist-dominant West Germany absorb communist East Germany, and in doing so, left behind some of the more progressive elements of GDR society, including closer wage parity between genders and abortion rights.

For many eastern Germans, reunification also came with a sense that their institutions, careers and social arrangements had been swept aside rather than incorporated into a genuinely shared country. The economic shock was especially acute after the privatisation and closure of many East German enterprises.

Around the 30th anniversary of reunification, the Bertelsmann Foundation published a study based on research by the Berlin institute pollytix. It revealed that 84 percent of eastern respondents felt the unified nation should have kept more elements that worked well in the GDR. Researchers noted that Easterners frequently expressed that a true common society was never created, feeling instead that the Western system was simply imposed upon them.

The upheaval coincided with a surge in racist violence. In Rostock-Lichtenhagen in 1992, several hundred far-right rioters attacked the Sunflower House, which included accommodation for Vietnamese contract workers, and threw Molotov cocktails as police failed for days to regain control. This and other xenophobic attacks reflected the wider discontent non-white people faced as Germany sought to unify amid rising economic uncertainty.

Similar anti-immigration debates and economic fears have fuelled the rise of the far-right Alternative for Deutschland party in recent years.

For Guetinger, the enforced separation he has witnessed, first in his own life and then with his wife’s family, has left a legacy not just for his generation, but also for his children, both of whom were born during the division.

“There is a very famous saying – that you tear down the Wall, but there is still the ‘Mauer im Kopf’, or wall in the mind. I think my children’s generation are affected by this but in a very different way. They know there are these frictions.

“Even now, it’s very difficult to see how the division has affected my life. It feels like a daydream. History has taught us that politics does not work well if people are forced to separate. People should be free. Who are the people to say you are not allowed to meet your own family?

“My experiences have shown me that it’s abnormal to keep people separated and divided.”

articles.title: Man leaves young son on Mount Fuji before ascending Japan’s highest peak
articles.excerpt:
Boy, seven, had complained of feeling tired so father left him with snacks and a soft drink and continued his climb

A man who abandoned his seven-year-old son on Mount Fuji in Japan after the boy com...
articles.body_text:
Boy, seven, had complained of feeling tired so father left him with snacks and a soft drink and continued his climb

A man who abandoned his seven-year-old son on Mount Fuji in Japan after the boy complained of feeling tired while on a family hike has been reprimanded by local police.

A worker on Japan’s highest mountain discovered the child sitting alone on a bench near the sixth station of the Fujinomiya trail at an altitude of more than 2,000 metres (6,500 feet) on Thursday.

After inviting the boy to take shelter at the station, the worker called the police, who took the child into protective custody.

It emerged that he had told his father he was too tired to continue while they were hiking up the trail in the early hours of the morning.

The man, who was from Japan’s fourth-largest city, Nagoya, gave his son some snacks and a soft drink.

He then told him to wait for him before continuing his five-hour ascent to the summit with the child’s older brother, who had already gone on ahead. It would have taken him about eight hours to return, according to local reports.

By the time police officers managed to contact the boy’s father, he had ascended to the eighth station, a three-hour hike from where he had left his son.

They told him to turn back, and after reuniting him with his son reprimanded him for leaving the child alone on an active volcano.

“Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable,” officers said, according to Japan Today.

Weather on the mountain, which has its own microclimate, is unpredictable and can change rapidly. Hypothermia poses a serious risk for hikers even in the summer.

The father is said to have apologised to the police, saying: “I made a rash decision, and I deeply regret it.”

Local police are urging hikers to consider the abilities and stamina of everyone in their group when planning an ascent on Mount Fuji, and to adjust their pace accordingly.

articles.title: Andy Burnham says he wants to bring men’s World Cup back to UK in 2042
articles.excerpt:
PM tells regional mayors he is keen for tournament to be played in British Isles  for first time since 1966

Andy Burnham has said he wants to bring the men’s World Cup to the UK in 2042, returning th...
articles.body_text:
PM tells regional mayors he is keen for tournament to be played in British Isles  for first time since 1966

Andy Burnham has said he wants to bring the men’s World Cup to the UK in 2042, returning the tournament to Britain for the first time in almost eight decades.

At a meeting in No 10 North in Manchester on Friday, the prime minister told regional mayors he was keen for the tournament to be played in the British Isles.

When the 1966 World Cup took place in England, with the home side beating West Germany 4-2 in the final after extra time, it was the only time the country has either hosted or won the contest.

Burnham, a keen football fan who has a season ticket at Everton, said earlier this month that it was “insane” only one World Cup had been held anywhere in the UK.

It is understood a formal application to stage the competition could also involve other home nations, none of which have ever hosted any World Cup games.

In recent years, joint bids between countries for major football tournaments have become more common. Alongside the Republic of Ireland, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will host the men’s European championships in 2028.

A Downing Street source said: “We support the FA’s priorities in terms of the tournaments they are already hosting, and any others they’d like to bid for.

“It would always be great to host more tournaments. These are broad aspirations – it’s a general ambition. The prime minister is a sports fan and loves his football.”

England made a doomed bid to host the 2018 World Cup, which was awarded to Russia amid allegations of corruption.

In 2014, while serving in the shadow cabinet, Burnham said he was uncomfortable that the tournament was still allowed to take place in Russia after its annexation of Crimea.

Under Fifa regulations, no European country would be eligible to stage the World Cup until 2042.

In 2000, Fifa introduced rules that meant the tournament would be rotated around its six continental confederations. It led to South Africa hosting its first World Cup in 2010, but the strict system was scrapped in October 2007.

Nations are not allowed to bid to stage a World Cup if either of the previous two tournaments have taken place on the same continent.

The 2030 World Cup will be hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, with some early matches taking place in South America to mark the tournament’s centenary. The first World Cup was played in Uruguay in 1930.

Fifa has also confirmed that the 2034 tournament will take place in Saudi Arabia. The location of the 2038 World Cup has not yet been announced, but under the rules, games are likely to be played in North America or Oceania, which includes Australia and New Zealand.

At Friday’s meeting, Burnham is also understood to have spoken about the possibility of hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the north of England in the 2040s.

Earlier this year, under the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, UK Sport was commissioned to assess whether a bid would be viable.

It is understood that the government is considering the possibility of a “multi-city bid” in an attempt to spread any economic benefit between several northern cities.

articles.title: Russian strikes kill 6 people in Ukraine, day after shopping complex attack
articles.excerpt: Russian aerial strikes on Ukraine have killed at least six people and injured 26 others, while a Ukrainian drone attack hit a house in southern Russia, killing two children and injuring their parents,...
articles.body_text:
Russian aerial strikes on Ukraine have killed at least six people and injured 26 others, while a Ukrainian drone attack hit a house in southern Russia, killing two children and injuring their parents, officials on both sides said.

Kyiv’s Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed on Saturday morning that one person was killed in a warehouse fire in the Darnytskyi district following an overnight Russian ballistic missile attack.

In the Kherson region, three others were killed and 13 wounded after Russian strikes damaged homes and apartment buildings, the regional military administration reported.

In Donetsk region, Russian attacks left one person dead and seven wounded, including five in the front-line city of Kramatorsk, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin, local media reported. In the Sumy region, a drone strike on a house killed one man, while six others were hurt in separate drone attacks across the region, regional officials said, according to reports.

In the city of Kherson itself, a drone strike set a shopping centre ablaze, though no casualties were reported, reports said.

On the other side, in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, authorities said two children were killed and two adults wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike.

The latest attacks coincided with ongoing rescue operations in Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown, where emergency workers searched the charred wreckage of the Sunny Gallery shopping complex following Friday afternoon’s assault.

Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the Kryvyi Rih Defense Council, said Russian forces targeted the city’s largest shopping centre with jet-powered Shahed drones.

A second wave hit roughly 30 minutes after the first on Friday, allegedly targeting emergency crews responding to the scene.

Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha confirmed in an update on Saturday morning that the death toll in Kryvyi Rih had risen to 16, with more than 130 wounded, including 22 children.

Zelenskyy called Friday’s attack “absolutely cynical and despicable” and an “act of barbarism”, promising a swift response. “Attacks like these are nothing less than terrorist acts,” he posted on Telegram.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said Friday’s attack began “at 4:30 in the afternoon when the mall is typically crowded,” with a second wave following “just 30 minutes later, with rescue workers from nearby regions called in to help”.

“The attacks come as civilian casualties in the war continue to mount, with July marking one of the deadliest months for civilians on both sides since the full-scale war began. And they are another example of how attacks far beyond the front lines are taking their toll on ordinary people,” she said.

articles.title: Canada vows to match Trump’s 50% tariffs after trade deal talks fail
articles.excerpt:
Mark Carney accuses Washington of ‘unfair’ last-minute changes to deal, as US and Canada fail to reach agreement after three-day extension of talks

Canadian prime minister Mark Carney has promised to...
articles.body_text:
Mark Carney accuses Washington of ‘unfair’ last-minute changes to deal, as US and Canada fail to reach agreement after three-day extension of talks

Canadian prime minister Mark Carney has promised to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar”, after the two sides failed to agree a trade deal by the deadline of midnight on Friday.

Canadian officials had worked hard in good faith but “last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal”, Carney said in a statement.

He said of the 50% tariffs the US was imposing: “Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.”

The US tariffs will affect about US$20bn worth of Canadian products after the last-ditch negotiations failed to resolve the latest strain in already tense relations between the historic allies.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer said the breakdown represented a “missed opportunity for Canada”.

“Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week,” he said in the statement shortly before midnight on Friday.

“Despite the US offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days.”

Greer said the US offer was “forward-looking” and included “a historic economic and national security partnership”.

The retaliation escalates the two countries’ trade conflict and calls into question the future of a North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico that is crucial to industry in all three countries.

Donald Trump’s import taxes will hit about 5% of what Canada ships to the US every year, including products ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.

Canada sought concessions on steel, aluminum, vehicles and lumber that the US was unwilling to provide, a senior Trump administration official told reporters.

The political impact of the breakdown will likely be even bigger than the economic fallout. The countries sold each other $880bn worth of goods and services last year.

The tariffs were initially supposed to kick in at 12.01am Wednesday but Trump extended the deadline for three days to allow talks to continue. No further talks have been planned.

Carney said his government would announce additional support for Canadian workers and businesses in the coming days, and that Canada’s goal throughout the negotiations had been to secure the best possible agreement, “never a deal at any price or on any deadline”.

The move was supported by Ontario premier Doug Ford, who said on X: “Team Canada needs to stand together more united than ever before. The prime minister has my full support for a strong response – tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar. As we fight to protect Canadian sovereignty and economic security, everything needs to be on the table. Ontario is ready to do its part.”

Candace Laing, president and CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, called the tariffs “a body blow to North American competitiveness”, warning they would raise costs for Americans while threatening Canadian customers, investment and small businesses.

With Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Battery fires at recycling centres are costing UK £1bn a year, figures show
articles.excerpt:
Experts say fires caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those  in vapes, are putting lives at risk

Fires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries such as th...
articles.body_text:
Experts say fires caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those  in vapes, are putting lives at risk

Fires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries such as those found in vapes are occurring at the rate of more than 10 a week, according to new figures.

Experts say the sheer volume of battery fires now occurring at waste facilities has reached a crisis that is putting lives at risk, costing £1bn a year and frustrating fire chiefs.

In figures shared with the Guardian, the Environment Services Association (ESA), the trade body for waste management companies, said its members had reported 1,518 fires in the year to March 2026. At least 541 of these fires were directly attributed to lithium ion batteries, the survey found. There were a further 216 battery fires in bin lorries.

The ESA said the reported number of battery-related fires underestimated the scale of the problem, because in most incidents it was impossible to determine the cause of the blaze. A spokesperson said: “We know 40% of fires at recycling centres are caused by batteries, but we think the actual number is more like 70%.”

It estimates that annual cost of these fires has increased from £150m in 2021 to £1bn today. The cause of this week’s blaze at a recycling centre in Deptford, south-east London, has yet to be determined. It was the latest in a series of fires at recycling centre and bin lorries, many of which have been blamed on batteries, particularly those in vapes. They include: Ilford in east London; Caerwent in Monmouthshire; Widnes in Cheshire; Glasgow; Costessey near Norwich, and Dereham in Norfolk.

Fire chiefs have been alarmed by the rise in this type of blaze and the resources needed to put them out.

After the Ilford fire, which took 25 firefighters to control, a spokesperson for London fire brigade said: “We’ve seen a growing number of fires at waste disposal sites that are believed to have been caused by a lithium battery.”

“Fires that we attend at sites like recycling centres and scrap yards can be very time consuming for our firefighters and often require a high level of resources to put the fire out. We’ve also seen the detrimental environmental and societal impact these fires can have on local communities.”

Dr Francesco Restuccia, a fire expert at King’s College London, said: “There has been exponential increase in fires at recycling centres, mainly because we are using and discarding lithium batteries in everyday objects like smartphones, children’s toys, toothbrushes and vapes. If they are not disposed off properly there’s a high chance of ignition.”

Explaining what happens when a lithium battery gets crushed, Restuccia said: “If the separator is pierced – which happens a lot at recycling centres – it creates a lot of internal short circuits in the battery, causing the temperature to increase until it reaches ignition point.”

The ESA commissioned the Health and Safety Executive to test what happens when a vape battery is punctured while next to paper and card. Video of the experiment, shared with the Guardian, showed the vape igniting like a sparkler and setting alight the paper and card. Temperatures of the vape reached more 750C in the experiment and became hot enough to ignite paper for two minutes.

The ESA hopes the experiment will demonstrate the need to safely dispose vapes to policymakers and the public. The waste management company Biffa said it has recovered 500,000 vapes at its facilities this summer alone.

The ESA is calling for a £5 deposit scheme on the sale of all vapes to ensure that vape users have an incentive to return used devices to retailers for safe disposal.

Patrick Brighty, the head of recycling policy at the ESA, said: “Battery fires are reaching epidemic proportions across Britain’s recycling and waste industry, placing workers at risk and threatening vital infrastructure upon which we all rely every day.

“It only takes a single battery hidden in household rubbish or recycling to cause a huge fire and decimate a facility. The total cost of battery fires now exceeds £1bn a year, with huge knock-on implications for insurance costs.

“Vapes are among the biggest culprits because they’re cheap, abundant and typically have a short use-life. ESA and others across our industry are calling on the government to implement a mandatory deposit scheme for vapes to incentivise users to return them safely back to the point of purchase so they can be recycled properly and away from other waste.”

articles.title: ‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account
articles.excerpt:
Couple considering suing for wrongful death after coroner found disciplinary process materially contributed to suicide

When a coroner ruled this month that the Treasury “materially contributed” to Ch...
articles.body_text:
Couple considering suing for wrongful death after coroner found disciplinary process materially contributed to suicide

When a coroner ruled this month that the Treasury “materially contributed” to Chloe Moffat’s death, her parents breathed out in bittersweet relief. For a year, David and Anne Moffat had been forced to become detectives in the worst case any parent could have to solve: why their daughter took her own life.

Chloe, 26, went to her job as a personal assistant at the Treasury on a Monday last May “happy as Larry” after a weekend she’d told her friends was a “10 out of 10”. She was planning a holiday with her sister, Alice, and arranging for friends to come for a dinner party the next weekend. She was, according to her father, living “the best life”.

That afternoon, however, she was sent to a surprise disciplinary meeting with her manager and her manager’s manager, which the coroner found left her distressed and convinced she was going to lose her job. The following morning, Chloe was dead.

Anne, 64, who is retired and used to work as the head of care at a children’s hospice, said: “When she first did it, we had to question Chloe. We had to question what might have driven Chloe to this.” She paused, and David added: “Criminality? Fraud? All sorts of things. Because why would somebody take their own life if they were the person that we expected?”

Anne interjected: “Are they on drugs? Are they in debt? Everything. And so we searched and questioned our own daughter.”

None of this was the case. After trawling through emails, talking to Chloe’s friends and colleagues and holding the Treasury to account in a gruelling, multi-day coroner’s court hearing, they found out their daughter had been mistreated by her employer.

“After our investigations, it was clear it was literally that one-to-one meeting,” Anne said. “Chloe never recovered. She walked out of that meeting absolutely destroyed and never recovered and went down a black hole.”

Speaking from their house in the French Alps, which they bought to be near Alice, who lives there and recently had a daughter, the couple seem exhausted. If the Moffats had not fought their daughter’s case, it is likely the coroner would have explained Chloe’s death with one word: suicide. Instead, she made a narrative finding, explaining the circumstances that led up to the death and laying blame partly at the Treasury’s door.

Since that finding two weeks ago, the Moffats have had no contact from the Treasury to offer condolences or an apology. “Now that the inquest has said that the coroner has found them responsible for Chloe’s death, we would have expected for them to have written to us,” David said.

Chloe was described as cheerful, popular and funny, and a person who took her job seriously. “I think Chloe was always looking to serve,” David said. Anne added: “I didn’t realise, but people like Chloe, who are bright, confident perfectionists, when they’re given a piece of shocking news such as they might lose their job, can be very vulnerable.”

The young woman was blindsided after being presented with anonymous complaints that she had shared confidential information at work, which she denied. She was not reassured that her job was safe even though she was unlikely to be dismissed, or offered a third party in the meeting to give her support or advice.

“If Chloe had known that it shouldn’t have happened, if she’d known her rights, she could have walked in and said: ‘I’m not having this meeting’, and walked out. But of course she didn’t. She didn’t know that, she was a people pleaser,” David said.

The coroner found Chloe was denied her rights at work, such as being told what the likely outcome of the disciplinary process would have been, which was a written warning, and that she could bring a supporter with her. Instead, she felt ambushed and was convinced she would lose the job she had worked so hard for.

Anne said: “I don’t know about the original complaints about Chloe, if they were malicious or to bring her down a peg or two – she was a big personality in the office.”

Her parents are considering suing the Treasury for wrongful death, particularly as they have had no response from the ministry since the finding. “If that’s the only way we’re going to get recognition, it’s a possibility,” David said.

The Treasury is obliged to give the coroner a response to the prevention of future deaths report she issued to the civil service. The coroner found there was a risk of further deaths at the Treasury because of how the department handled disciplinary cases.

The department brought a team of lawyers to the inquest, who pushed for Chloe’s death to be recorded as an unexplained suicide.

“We definitely want to be in touch with the Treasury because we do want Chloe remembered for the Chloe that she was,” Anne said. “And be that a bench in her name or whatever, but we want her to be remembered, but we do fear that she is going to be brushed under the carpet and lessons will not be learned.”

Unusually for an inquest, the small, drab room in Surrey was full of young people in their early to mid-20s – Chloe’s friends and colleagues, who wept throughout. Those who attended from the Treasury were not given bereavement leave to attend the inquest into their friend’s death. “They didn’t get any time off from the Treasury or support for that horrible ordeal they had gone through,” Anne said.

The couple said they hoped the Treasury acknowledged Chloe and issued a satisfactory response to the prevention of future deaths report, so this nightmarish chapter could be closed and they could begin to grieve.

“We need to grieve. And I’m not sure that we have. I think the inquest has delayed that,” Anne said.

David said: “The hole it’s left in our lives is just enormous. We’re only still coming to terms with that. Sometimes we don’t feel we can attend family events because we’ve got something missing. We are a tight-knit family, we’ve all holidayed together. But now we don’t have Chloe.”

They said they hoped Chloe’s case could help prevent other parents from going through the same experience. And they wanted to remember their daughter as the grinning, popular, confident, adventurous woman she was.

“We have got so many happy memories. So that’s what we have to be positive about,” Anne said. “I think: ‘At least she didn’t have cancer,’ you know, and suffer. She was literally happy up until that meeting.”

David said: “I think for sure we will continue to want to ensure that we spread the word of what we have learned from all this.”

A Treasury spokesperson said: “Our deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s family, and the department continues to mourn Chloe’s death.

“We are taking all concerns extremely seriously and are considering the coroner’s findings carefully. We have introduced improvements to guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements but recognise we must continue to take action to prevent this happening again.”

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

articles.title: Sorrow as community pays tribute to ‘shining light’ Lily Hooper after NSW hiking tragedy
articles.excerpt:
The 18-year-old remembered as a talented athlete with an infectious smile and ‘one of those people who everyone simply liked’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Tributes hav...
articles.body_text:
The 18-year-old remembered as a talented athlete with an infectious smile and ‘one of those people who everyone simply liked’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Tributes have flowed for 18-year-old Lily Hooper, remembered as an adventurous, multitalented athlete with an infectious smile, after her body was found on Thursday afternoon, eight days after she disappeared while hiking in the New South Wales southern highlands.

The teenager was a fixture across local sporting and community groups in the Wollondilly region, training in martial arts, alongside her job as a Sydney BridgeClimb guide.

In her home town of Oakdale, the community gathered for a vigil on Friday evening at Willis park. By Saturday morning, the park fence was adorned with flowers, fairy lights and electric candles.

The Wollondilly Performing Arts Centre and the shire library were illuminated in purple. The mayor, Matt Gould, said on Friday that the community had rarely been as devastated.

This article includes content provided by Facebook. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

“From 5pm this afternoon and across the weekend, Willis Park at Oakdale will become a place for our community to come together and remember Lily Hooper,” Gould said, adding that Red Cross volunteers were on site “to support anyone who may need someone to talk to”.

“[It’s] just an opportunity for everyone to come together and show the level of support there is for the family, and just to look out for each other.”

Flags across the region, including at the Oakdale Rural Fire Service, flew at half mast. The brigade said in a statement that the community is navigating a “deep sorrow … as we all remember the shining light that has touched so many of us”.

This article includes content provided by Facebook. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Hooper trained at Toodokan Self Defence Academy, which cancelled classes on Thursday afternoon after the news. The academy said in a tribute that Lily was “a beautiful soul, taken far too soon”.

This article includes content provided by Facebook. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Her martial arts instructor, Mark Szalajko, said he would miss her smile and conversation, describing her as a talented, tough fighter.

“She was a talented and tough martial artist, but despite that toughness, Lily was such a lovely person. She was one of those people who everyone simply liked,” he said. “I will really miss her smile, her conversations and the moments we shared on the mat.”

Further tributes came from the Oaks Netball Club, which said it was “devastated by the loss”, with members to wear black armbands in her memory at games over the weekend.

This article includes content provided by Facebook. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

The Burragorang District Soccer Club also posted a tribute on social media in Hooper’s honour: “Our community has lost a truly beautiful person, and our hearts are heavy with sadness.”

Hooper’s high school, Campbelltown Performing Arts – where she graduated in 2025 – remembered her as a “kind, humorous and respectful young woman who lit up every room with her infectious smile, positive energy and determination to live life to its fullest”.

This article includes content provided by Facebook. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

“I am so proud of the woman you became … You are so loved my musical angel,” one commenter wrote under the school’s tribute.

Another commented “I feel incredibly privileged to have known her and to have shared so many memorable moments with her. What I will remember most is the loyalty she had for her beautiful best friends.”

Sydney Harbour BridgeClimb, where Hooper worked as a guide, issued a statement saying she was “an absolute delight from the moment she joined and lit up every space with her smile and enthusiasm”.

“She was compassionate, a friend to all, motivated and had a positive impact on everyone she connected with,” a spokesperson said. “Her loss is felt deeply throughout our team, and Lily’s family and loved ones are in our thoughts and our hearts, today and always.”

Police initially told Hooper’s family she was alive, with footage circulated by Channel Seven showing the elation of friends and family. Her father, Jim Hooper, showed off a guitar and packet of Tim Tams he had brought to the site “because it might lure her out of the bush”. Hope was shattered barely 30 minutes later.

The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, later told reporters in Goulburn that the devastating miscommunication was “born out of elation”.

“Tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation, and obviously, we know now, an impact on her family,” Lanyon said.

The assistant commissioner Joseph Cassar told reporters in Moss Vale on Thursday afternoon that the searchers had carried handheld radios and faced communication challenges in the “thick, dense terrain”.

Hooper, an experienced hiker, had been found dead off the trail, a “significant distance” from her car.

The Wollondilly Rotary Club established a fundraiser to support the Hooper family after her disappearance.

“Lily’s kindness, spirit, and connection to the Oakdale and Wollondilly regions, along with her family, has touched many lives, and our club is committed to standing beside her family during this difficult time,” the club said in a statement.

articles.title: Coles website down after viral Reddit post sees customers buy cases of alcoholic drinks at nearly 80% discount
articles.excerpt:
Supermarket’s website and app go offline as customers save more than $100 on some 24-packs

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Coles website and app have gone offline hou...
articles.body_text:
Supermarket’s website and app go offline as customers save more than $100 on some 24-packs

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Coles website and app have gone offline hours after a viral Reddit post highlighted a nearly 80% discount on 24-packs of premixed alcoholic drinks.

For several hours on Saturday, both the Coles website and app displayed a message advising “we’re currently offline – but not for long”. The website and app came back online, before the website went down again during the afternoon. It was back up at about 4pm AEST.

It came after a post by an Australian Reddit account on Friday about a discount on 24-packs of Jack Daniel’s & Cola 330ml bottles sold via Coles by subsidiary Liquorland which were marked down from $130 to $27, a saving of $103, or just under 80%.

“Found this. I’m assuming it’s a mistake?!” wrote the account, which is run by the operators of price tracking website CW Scanner.

They subsequently noticed similar discounts, lowering the price of 24-packs of premixed drinks and beer to a price similar to that of discounted four- or six-packs.

The operators of CW Scanner told Guardian Australia that the post had received more than 180,000 views. Other users described ordering online with the discounts, which did not appear on the Liquorland website itself, with one having it matched at their local liquor store.

But on Saturday, Reddit users noticed the Coles website had gone down, while some later wrote that their orders had been cancelled by Coles. The Coles website and app came back online briefly on Saturday afternoon, with the beer and premixed drinks categories removed. The website subsequently went offline again.

In a statement on Saturday afternoon, a Coles spokesperson said it was aware of a technical issue affecting its website and app, and “was working quickly to restore services”.

“Due to a technical error, select 24-pack beer and RTD [ready-to-drink] products were incorrectly priced on our website,” they said.

“The error has been corrected, and impacted customers are being notified. Any customers charged for the affected items will be refunded in accordance with our normal refund process. We apologise for the error and any inconvenience caused.”

The operators of CW Scanner told Guardian Australia they suspected the discounts may be a mistake made by AI integrated into Coles’ platforms.

“If the AI was deeply integrated into the system it might explain why they had to take the entire site offline,” a CW Scanner representative told Guardian Australia.

“It seems to be something like a wildcard term was used to search for all 4-packs which found 24-packs as well.”

CW Scanner identified at least 20 24-packs – or cartons – of beer and 46 cases of premixed drinks affected by the discounts, with the average discount on beer about $49, and premixed drinks $111.

The largest discount, on 24-packs of Smirnoff Crush Mango & Peach Zero Sugar 6% 440ml cans, provided a saving of $173, down to $29 from $202.

Using data from CW Scanner, the Guardian has reported that promotional prices switched on and off at Coles and Woolworths largely in sync over the past two years.

Earlier this year, a court found Coles’ “Down Down” promotions in some cases falsely led customers to believe they were enjoying a true price reduction.

articles.title: China’s new moon mission could unlock secret of lunar ice: Why that matters
articles.excerpt:
China is set to launch its Chang’e-7 unmanned, robotic space mission, possibly as early as Monday morning, to look for ice water in the permanently shadowed craters of the moon’s south pole.

This mar...
articles.body_text:
China is set to launch its Chang’e-7 unmanned, robotic space mission, possibly as early as Monday morning, to look for ice water in the permanently shadowed craters of the moon’s south pole.

This marks China’s seventh and most ambitious moon mission so far. Here is what we know about it.

The Chang’e‑7 launch window runs from Monday, August 24 to Monday, August 31, according to launch observers. That means the mission could lift off on any day in that period.

The Chang’e-7 comprises an orbiter, a lander, a rover and a hopper.

Over the past two decades, several space missions have established that there is water on the moon.

Since the 1960s, even before the first Apollo landing in 1969, scientists speculated that water could exist on the moon. However, when Apollo crews returned samples for testing in the late 1960s and early 1970s, they appeared to be dry.

Finally, in 2009, NASA deliberately crashed a rocket segment and its probe into a shadowed lunar crater to analyse the dust plume it kicked up. This provided one of the clearest direct confirmations that significant ice water does exist on the moon, building on earlier detections of water and hydrogen by probes.

In October 2020, NASA scientists announced that water on the moon is more widespread than previously known. They said water molecules had been found to be encapsulated within mineral grains on the lunar surface and speculated that more water is hidden in ice patches which are in permanent shadows.

NASA describes these permanent shadows as dark areas inside deep craters near the north and south poles of the moon where sunlight has not reached for millions or even billions of years. In 2018, prior to confirming it in 2020, NASA had detected water ice in shadowed parts of the moon through mapping.

Expanding knowledge about water on the moon is vital because ancient polar ice may have preserved a record of lunar volcanic activity and of water delivered by comets and asteroids to the Earth-moon system, offering clues to how our own oceans originally formed.

Additionally, if there is enough water on the moon that is realistically accessible, it could serve as a source of drinking water for crewed lunar missions, and could also help to keep equipment cool.

Hydrogen could also be extracted from moon water to provide fuel, while oxygen could be extracted to breathe, supporting onward missions to Mars or lunar mining.

The 1967 United Nations Outer Space Treaty bans any nation from claiming sovereignty over the moon or owning it as territory. It does not explicitly prohibit commercial operations, but it requires private activities in space to be authorised and supervised by states and leaves key questions about resource ownership unresolved.

In 2023, Russia’s lunar spacecraft, Luna-25, was launched to look for frozen water in the moon’s south pole. However, the Luna-25 spun out of control and crashed. The crash prevented any scientific data collection or water discovery.

Racing against the Luna-25 mission was India’s Chandrayaan-3, which also aimed to expand knowledge of lunar water ice. Chandrayaan-3 successfully landed in August 2023 and found critical new evidence of water on the surface of the moon’s south pole through soil temperature readings.

Attempted landings at the moon’s south pole have failed before because of its challenging terrain, which is full of craters and deep trenches.

The south pole is far from the equatorial region targeted by previous missions, including the crewed Apollo landings.

The upcoming Chang’e-7 is aiming to expand knowledge about where, exactly, water is located in the craters of the moon, how deep it is, what form it is in and whether it is indeed possible to access it.

The Chang’e-7’s six-legged hopper has been designed to jump into and out of the deep, shadowed craters near the south pole that are hard for traditional rovers to reach, to look for water ice and other resources.

No previous space mission has used a dedicated hopper to jump in and out of lunar craters in this way.

articles.title: ‘It was a tsunami’: Floods leave death trail in India’s Assam
articles.excerpt: Assam, India – Debiram Panika, a 37-year-old daily wage labourer from northeastern India’s Assam state, would speak to his wife and two daughters on video calls every day from Dimapur, a town in neigh...
articles.body_text:
Assam, India – Debiram Panika, a 37-year-old daily wage labourer from northeastern India’s Assam state, would speak to his wife and two daughters on video calls every day from Dimapur, a town in neighbouring Nagaland state where he worked.

But when his phone rang at about 11am on July 19, there was panic in the voice of his 30-year-old wife, Dipika.

“I could only see my wife telling me on the video call, ‘This is it for us. We are going to die,’ before the call was disconnected,” Panika recalled, speaking to Al Jazeera.

It was the last time they spoke. Moments later, rising waters from the nearby Dikhow River, which snakes past their village in Assam’s Sivasagar district, surged into their bamboo-and-mud home with a ferocious current and swept away Dipika and four-year-old daughter Radhika.

“The water came flooding like sea waves, and they were gone in a flash,” Panika said, as he stood in front of the ruined home he has since returned to.

Sivasagar is part of the eastern Assam region, also referred to as Upper Assam. Incessant rains between July 18 and July 20 submerged the region and the neighbouring Naga Hills of Nagaland.

Monsoon floods usually impact northern and western Assam, and parts of central Assam, the worst. But several Nagaland districts bordering Upper Assam received heavy rainfall on those three days, leading to dozens of landslides. This intense run-off swelled Naga Hills-origin rivers and caused devastation downstream.

The resultant floods killed more than 100 people, destroyed 2,700 villages, and displaced 700,000 people across the state. The state government says 1.2 million people were impacted in all, their lives disrupted.

Most waters have since receded, but Radhika’s body is yet to be found.

“I look for Radhika every day in the bushes, tirelessly,” Panika said, holding back his tears. “Her last words, calling me ‘Papa’, are still reverberating in my ears.”

Panika’s other daughter, Ridhika, 10, was at a relative’s place a few metres away when her mother and sister were swept away by the flood. Ridhika held onto a bamboo bush and was later rescued by locals.

Several riverine villages in Sivasagar have been wrecked by debris carried down by the waters of the Dikhow from the surrounding Naga Hills.

Tens of thousands of tree trunks lie piled up in places that used to be homes, as lush rice fields, the main source of livelihood, have been washed away.

Kukil Das, a 30-year-old Facebook vlogger in Debiram’s village of Nepali Khuti, told Al Jazeera that “the torrent of the flood was like an apocalyptic event seen in the movies.

“Trees as tall as 30 to 40 metres (100-130ft) came down from the hills, flooding the river, and wiped out everything as they crashed against our homes,” he said. “There is no home left. It was a tsunami.”

Das and his friend Shravan Prasad, from the neighbouring Bihubor village, said they saved at least 1,000 lives by using boats the two villages had at that time.

“We put together a group of friends with the seven boats and started rescuing people turn by turn for two days and nights without food and water,” Prasad said.

Das said the floods forced residents to take shelter on the roofs of concrete homes they could find, as cries for help and the sounds of the river washing away homes echoed in the neighbourhood.

Laxmi Sharma, who owned one such concrete house, said she provided shelter to at least 60 people on her terrace after the river water gushed into Nepali Khuti.

“People ran towards the roof of my building. We thought we were going to die,” Sharma, 46, told Al Jazeera. “But it is a miracle that we are still alive even though my house was barely out of water.”

Not everyone could escape the flood’s wrath, though.

In Sivasagar’s Simaluguri village, two friends – Reihana Ahmed, a Muslim, and Ratul Swarna, a Hindu, both in their 30s – were swept away in the torrent.

When Ahmed, a mother of two, was drowning as the deluge entered her village, Swarna, who did not know how to swim, jumped to save her without thinking about his life.

The two friends were later found dead in the paddy fields. “It was humanity that won in a disaster like this,” Ahmed’s husband Aminul Haque said with a sorrowful smile.

Besides the eroding banks of the Dikhow River in Prajabasti, another flood-affected village, 75-year-old Asor Ali sat in disbelief next to his wife, Jamila Khatun.

“Even the generations preceding me have not seen a flood like this,” he said, staring at the flowing river. “Even the 1950s earthquake that triggered the floods here did not do so much damage.”

A magnitude 8.6 earthquake hit Assam and Tibet across the border in 1950, altering the region’s riverine system. Nearly 5,000 people died. Since then, Assam has witnessed frequent floods, which intensify during the monsoons, says Mirza Zulfiqur Rahman, a researcher on the basin of the Brahmaputra, the region’s major river: The Naga Hills rivers that flooded Upper Assam are its tributaries.

But residents say this year’s deadly deluge is not just a natural phenomenon.

Biren Gogoi, 43, says rampant stone and sand mining in regional rivers, coupled with aggressive deforestation and coal extraction in Nagaland’s Mon district, triggered the devastation.

Global Nature Watch, an open-source online platform that provides real-time data on deforestation across the world, showed that Nagaland lost 14 percent of its tree cover between 2002 and 2025, with Mon district bordering Assam’s Sivasagar being the most affected.

According to the latest report published in 2023 by the Forest Survey of India, Nagaland has lost about 794.88 square kilometres (306.9 square miles) of forest cover between 2013 and 2023.

Al Jazeera travelled along the Assam-Nagaland border and saw signs of deforestation on the hills and mining activities in both the states. Satellite images also confirmed rampant coal mining in Nagaland’s Mon district, and stone mining crushers on Assam’s side, especially in Bihubor, one of the epicentres of the Assam flood.

While Mon’s Deputy Commissioner Wennyei Konyak acknowledged the possibility of illegal mining in the district, he added that the land was protected under Indian laws to uphold the rights of Indigenous tribes, and therefore government interference in the area was limited.

“I would not blame mining activities for the flood. It was just the wrath of nature,” he told Al Jazeera.

But experts and political leaders in Assam say mining played a direct role in the floods.

Debabrata Saikia of the opposition Congress party, who is the legislator from Sivasagar constituency, accused Assam’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of allowing illegal excavations for stone and sand on the Dikhow riverbank, resulting in a cratered wasteland that worsened the floods.

“This unchecked plundering of riverbeds and hills under the ruling government has engineered this into a man-made disaster,” Saikia told Al Jazeera.

Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, however, rejected the allegation on August 4, blaming excessive rainfall in Nagaland for triggering the Upper Assam deluge. On August 14, Ranoj Pegu, a cabinet minister in the state’s BJP government, blamed erratic rainfall due to climate change for the deluge.

Rahman, the Brahmaputra river basin researcher, believes that while the climate crisis played a role, the flood was “purely human-made”, caused by the fracturing of the landscape.

“The unrestrained stone extraction from the Dikhow riverbed has damaged the river’s natural cushion,” Rahman said. “That means the river loses the capacity to resist high flows of torrents that break embankments and cause floods.”

An official document from 2022, seen by Al Jazeera, also highlights mining as a factor in possible large-scale floods downstream on the Assam side.

Al Jazeera reached out to senior district officials in Sivasagar as well as state government officials for their comments on allegations of unchecked coal mining but did not get any response.

Back in Prajabasti village, Ali, the septuagenarian, is mentally preparing himself for future floods.

“It will happen again, so long as there is greed for land and coal in humans,” he said. “Nature pays them back.”

articles.title: Is this the end of Harry and Meghan’s American dream?
articles.excerpt:
The Sussexes are returning to the UK with significantly reduced media deals in an industry where fame alone can no longer guarantee success

Having settled in California in the aftermath of their dram...
articles.body_text:
The Sussexes are returning to the UK with significantly reduced media deals in an industry where fame alone can no longer guarantee success

Having settled in California in the aftermath of their dramatic decoupling from the royal family in 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex announced a partnership that appeared to set a clear destination for their new lives outside the House of Windsor.

With every global media stable clamouring for their signature, the couple revealed a deal with Netflix reportedly worth $100m. The ambitions were lofty and broad, including scripted and unscripted projects, shows for all ages and documentaries.

A $20m podcast deal with Spotify appeared to confirm their ambitions; the Sussexes were reinventing themselves in the competitive world of content creation, a media powerhouse in the booming universe of streaming and podcasting.

As the couple now prepare to return to the UK, they do so with those mega-deals either pared back or expired, and their media plans less clear. It raises the question: is this the end of their American dream?

As with all things Harry and Meghan-related, their various media forays have spawned copious amounts of reactionary content and commentary. Each appearance, commission and production has been dissected: there have been blockbuster hits, much-publicised misses and some brutal reviews along the way.

For Harry, the pull of returning to the UK, if perhaps not permanently, has been clear for a while.

He says he loves his country, and in an interview with the Guardian last year, he admitted he hankered for home.

“I have always loved the UK and I always will love the UK. It’s been good to reconnect with the causes I am passionate about. I have been able to spend some time with people that I have known for so long. It is hard to do it from far away.”

Perhaps more so recently because his father, King Charles, has been ill. And on the work front, it hasn’t been easy either.

Six years in the content game offers a case study in how difficult it can be to negotiate the shifting sands of a transformed media landscape, so difficult that even a Hollywood actor and a British prince are not guaranteed to succeed.

Those years have proved there is one bankable aspect of the Sussex brand: their relationship with the royal family continues to be devoured on an industrial scale. However, launching lifestyle brands and philanthropic pursuits that rely purely on name recognition – even with a packed contacts book of A-list friends to help – cannot guarantee reliable success in the cut-throat era of the attention economy.

“The Sussexes have kind of got caught up in the media’s awkward teenage transition,” said Evan Shapiro, a former US media executive turned leading analyst of the creator economy. “Just being famous is no longer enough … The last time Meghan Markle worked in show business [starring in the US legal drama Suits], it was a different era. It was top down: ‘We push it out, you watch it.’ That’s just how it worked.

“That era has passed. It’s fucking hard [now] … the competition is literally every human on earth. Eight billion people with phones who are all competing with Meghan Markle.”

The Sussexes could scarcely have had better timing for their eye-catching 2020 Netflix deal, via their Archewell Productions organisation – global streamers were scrambling for big names to lure subscribers.
