articles.title: Missing teen hiker Lily Hooper found dead as NSW police apologise for miscommunication ‘born of elation’
articles.excerpt:
Initial report from ‘thick and dense terrain’ where Hooper was located was she had been found alive but within 10 minutes a ‘more accurate account’ was relayed to police

Follow our Australia news liv...
articles.body_text:
Initial report from ‘thick and dense terrain’ where Hooper was located was she had been found alive but within 10 minutes a ‘more accurate account’ was relayed to police

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The body of missing 18-year-old bushwalker Lily Hooper has been found in a remote New South Wales national park more than a week after she set out on her hike.

Police have apologised “unreservedly” for wrongly suggesting Hooper had been alive when she was found by SES search volunteers off the walking trail in the state’s southern highlands on Thursday morning.

The assistant commissioner Joe Cassar said SES search volunteers initially reported at 11.30am that the teenager had been found alive in “thick and dense terrain” in Nattai national park about 90km south-west of Sydney.

However, within 10 minutes, the search crew relayed a “more accurate account” to police confirming Hooper was dead.

“There’s no playbook to communication,” Cassar told reporters in Moss Vale on Thursday afternoon.

Her body was not expected to be retrieved for many hours, NSW police said.

The commissioner, Mal Lanyon, told reporters in Goulburn on Thursday the miscommunication about Hooper being found was “born out of elation”.

“Tragically that miscommunication then led to a deflation and obviously, we know now, an impact on her family,” Lanyon said.

“I unashamedly apologise for any additional trauma that may have caused Lily’s family, but certainly for the embarrassment and confusion that caused.”

The assistant commissioner said Hooper’s parents had been at the search command post and were being kept “well informed” by police. The family was told of the initial report that Hooper was alive before the devastating update came through from the scene using hand-held radios.

“I cannot turn the clock back,” Cassar said. “If we were able to provide them more detailed information on that first report, I can tell you that would have been the case.”

Earlier on Thursday, police had told media a “hiker” had been found after the multi-agency search and the NSW premier, Chris Minns, told parliament Hooper had been “found alive” with half a bottle of water.

But a short time later, Minns announced: “I’ve got some terrible news. I apologise … Lily’s body has been found.”

Minns later said in a statement he had received incorrect advice and “genuinely believed” he was sharing good news. 
 “My deepest condolences are with Lily’s family,” the premier said. “I am profoundly sorry to think that anything I said may have added to their heartbreak at an already devastating time.”

Hooper was found off the trail a “significant distance” from her car, which was parked near the trail head on Wanganderry Road at High Range, Cassar said.

The assistant commissioner said it was not yet clear how she died or if she had sustained injuries. He said her body would likely be brought out by foot as air retrieval was “exceptionally difficult”.

A report will be prepared for the coroner, investigating the time, place and circumstances of Hooper’s death, as well as the search and communications issues. Cassar said criminal investigators from the Hume police district were gathering evidence in line with police protocol.

Hooper left her Sydney home on Wednesday 12 August for the hike. Initial police inquiries suggested she reached the summit of Bonnum Pic mountain mid-morning on Wednesday, having sent messages from the trail earlier that day.

She was reported missing when she did not return home that evening. Emergency services located her car late that night.

Lanyon said nearly 1,000 people had joined the search on the ground over the last week.

More than 100 ADF personnel had joined the search operation in the past 24 hours. The army personnel joined people from PolAir, NSW police, the SES, RFS, Fire and Rescue NSW, and the National Parks and Wildlife Service. A rescue helicopter and police helicopters were engaged.

Volunteers on the ground included Hooper’s family, family and Volunteer Rescue Association crews mobilised from as far north as Cessnock.

The SES said 260 volunteer members trained in bush search and rescue were on the ground from Saturday to Thursday.

On Monday, police said the search was focused on the lower sections of the Bonnum Pic walking trail. Police were uncertain what supplies Hooper had with her.

Police have said Hooper was believed to have been an experienced hiker.

The NSW police chief inspector Brendan Bernie said on Monday: “We’re hopefully relying on Lily’s experience to get her through this ordeal and [we] can locate her safely.”

Poor weather over the weekend had hampered search operations in the already complex terrain.

Outdoor recreation website AllTrails describes the Bonnum Pic hike as a “formidable challenge,” noting some hikers recommend using rope to negotiate “steep, exposed sections”.

“Post-fire regrowth has made the trail overgrown and difficult to identify … [and] the path frequently disappears,” the site’s description reads.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said on Thursday that Hooper’s death was an “unspeakable tragedy”.

“Lily Hooper had so much more to offer the world,” Albanese said.

“Her passing … will be felt very deeply across the southern highlands, among her family, her friends, and indeed right across the nation.”

Angus Taylor, the federal opposition leader and the local MP for the electorate where the Hooper family live, paid tribute, too.

“Any parent who reads this news will hug their children tighter tonight,” he said.

“When they do, they will spare a thought and a prayer for Lily’s mother, father, and family who can’t do the same. We grieve for their most terrible loss.”

articles.title: GCSE results: hundreds of thousands of pupils across England, Wales and Northern Ireland receive grades – latest updates
articles.excerpt:
Education secretary says the government is looking at changing the resits policy in England

Compulsory GCSE resits in England harm teenagers’ mental wellbeing, study finds

Lucy Powell said the gover...
articles.body_text:
Education secretary says the government is looking at changing the resits policy in England

Compulsory GCSE resits in England harm teenagers’ mental wellbeing, study finds

Lucy Powell said the government is looking at changing the resits policy in England, where students who have not achieved a grade 4 pass in English or maths GCSE are required to retake those exams.

As the Guardian’s education editor Richard Adams reported yesterday, research shows compulsory resits in England were having a negative impact on teenagers’ mental wellbeing. You can read Richard’s report here.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Powell said only one in five students who resit English and maths were passing them.

“For some, they’re doing it many times over,” she added. “So we’re branding them a failure after failure after failure. It’s knocking their confidence.

“It’s not giving them the passport that they need to go on to do something like an apprenticeship, or for others to go on to further study.”

She said the government is introducing a new “pathway qualification” at level one, which is below GCSEs at level two.

Powell said this would give “a high level of literacy and numeracy”, adding: “I want to work with employers so that it’s credible, so that that would be a sufficient gateway to get on to the next path.”

The British Academy, the national organisation for humanities and social sciences, said its analysis of GCSE results today shows business and psychology are up but languages face another year of decline.

French seeing its sharpest fall since 2018, with a 5.4% decrease in take-up this year.

Other modern languages, which includes Arabic, Chinese and Urdu among others, are also down by 4%.

Spanish growth may be slowing down, with a 0.3% increase compared to 2.6% last year and 6.2% the year before.

German is up 0.2%, a very small increase compared to its long-term decline of 12.5% over the past 5 years.

The highest growing subjects in Shape (the acronym for social sciences, humanities and arts) was business studies, with a 7.9% increase.

Sociology and psychology continue to rise, by 4.8% and 3% respectively.

Susan Smith, president of the British Academy, said: “This year’s GCSE entries show that young people continue to be inspired by subjects providing insight into people, economy and society.

double quotation markThe growth of business studies, sociology and psychology, in particular, show increasing appetite for skills nurtured by the social sciences, arts and humanities."

However, the continued fall in language entries is concerning. Languages are vital for diplomacy, trade and cultural understanding. AI translation is no match for the human communications skills and capabilities we need to navigate an increasingly interconnected, but divided and volatile world. Yet, losing languages at this level has a domino effect across the entire education system, and once this expertise disappears, it will be very hard to recover.

As government reflects on future education pathways, we urge ministers to seize every opportunity to give all young people access to a broad, balanced curriculum, delivering the critical thinking and creativity that employers value and the UK needs.”

Here are some statements from the prime minister and the education secretary on the GSCE results today.

double quotation markCongratulations to everyone collecting their results today, you should be proud of the hard work that got you here.

Whether the next step is sixth form, a college course, an apprenticeship, a T Level, work, or something else entirely, we’re ensuring that there are more opportunities than ever to choose your own path to get on in life. I’m determined to bring back hope and give every young person the chance to fulfil their potential.

double quotation markMassive congratulations to everyone collecting their results today – be proud of what it took to get here, and thank you to the teachers and families who backed you every step of the way.

More of you are hitting top grades in maths, and technical pass rates are climbing in every region. That’s proof there is no wrong door, only different routes that suit everyone’s individual ambition.

But there’s more to do to put academic and technical qualifications on an equal footing, so we’re introducing V Levels and expanding T Levels and apprenticeships, so wherever you’re headed next, there’s a path that works for you.”

Myles McGinley, managing director of the Cambridge OCR exam board, said more pupils are taking GCSE business studies than in previous years, describing this generation of young people as “increasingly entrepreneurial”.

He said business studies entries are a third higher than five years ago, adding: “The founders of some of the next great unicorn businesses may well be among those achieving GCSEs in business studies today.”

PE has also risen in popularity, McGinley said. “Are young people inspired by the successes of our athletes in recent years, from British Olympians to the Lionesses?”

Almost one in four boys in England received top grades in maths while results in English improved across the board, helping to propel improved GCSE results for this year’s cohort of 16-year-olds.

The stronger performances in maths helped pupils taking GCSEs in year 11 reach a record level for higher grades in England outside the Covid pandemic years, when exams were replaced by teacher assessments.

The overall results for 16-year-olds nudged slightly higher compared with last year, with the proportion receiving grades 7, 8 and 9 – equivalent to grades A and A* – rising by 0.1 of a percentage point to 23.1%. The proportion of nearly 700,000 16-year-olds in England who got a grade 4 or better – equivalent to a C or higher – also rose to 70.7%, compared with 70.5% in 2025.

Some of the strongest performances appeared to come in the compulsory subject of maths, where 22.3% received 7s or better, including 24% of boys and 20.5% of girls. But girls did worse than last year in lower grades, dropping from 71% awarded 4 and above to 70.7%, while boys improved further to 72.8%.

In case you need a reminder of the GCSE grading system in England, here’s what the numbers mean for those familiar with the old A-G letter system (which Wales and Northern Ireland still use):

Earlier this month, students in Scotland achieved record number of vocational and technical qualifications in their Nationals, Highers, Advanced Highers and Skills for Work Awards.

Pass rates for Scottish exams have increased as students across the country received their results. Figures show that the poverty-related attainment gap has narrowed compared with last year.

The National 5 (equivalent to GCSEs) pass rate rose by 0.8 percentage points in 2026, reaching a total of 79.2%. In 2025, the pass rate was 78.4%.

The pass rate for Highers was up 0.8% to 76.7% while Advanced Highers rose by 0.9% to 77.6%.

Admissions service Ucas said a record number of Scottish students aged 18 and under had been accepted into university or college. In total, 32,370 Scottish students of all ages secured places, up from 31,850 in 2025.

The prime minister has issued a message of support to students receiving their GCSE results today.

double quotation markCongratulations to everyone getting their GCSE results today, you should be proud of the work that got you here.

Whatever your results, remember there isn’t just one route to success.

We’re creating more opportunities for young people to choose the path that’s right for them, whether that’s academic or technical.

Every young person should have the chance to fulfil their potential. I’ll make sure they do.”

Lucy Powell said the government is looking at changing the resits policy in England, where students who have not achieved a grade 4 pass in English or maths GCSE are required to retake those exams.

As the Guardian’s education editor Richard Adams reported yesterday, research shows compulsory resits in England were having a negative impact on teenagers’ mental wellbeing. You can read Richard’s report here.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Powell said only one in five students who resit English and maths were passing them.

“For some, they’re doing it many times over,” she added. “So we’re branding them a failure after failure after failure. It’s knocking their confidence.

“It’s not giving them the passport that they need to go on to do something like an apprenticeship, or for others to go on to further study.”

She said the government is introducing a new “pathway qualification” at level one, which is below GCSEs at level two.

Powell said this would give “a high level of literacy and numeracy”, adding: “I want to work with employers so that it’s credible, so that that would be a sufficient gateway to get on to the next path.”

Education secretary Lucy Powell is on the media round this morning as students prepare to pick up their GCSE results, including her own daughter.

She said it was a “big day” that marks “a really important moment in a child’s progression”.

Speaking to Sky News, she added: “I know that the vast majority of young people have worked incredibly hard for these quite tough exams that they have faced over the summer, and what they will be getting today, hopefully, is a gateway to continue their study, to continue learning, to continue training and move on to the next stage in their life.”

She said plans to bring in new post-16 vocational qualifications would mean there is a “path for everybody”.

“I’m sure people today will feel proud of themselves, but they should be reassured that there is a pathway and there are options for them, and they need to make contact with their school or college and really talk about those options.”

Powell is due to visit a school later today, we will bring you the updates as soon as we get them.

The app allowing students to access their GCSE results digitally is being rolled out nationally this year, after a successful trial last year.

In 2025, nearly 100,000 year 11 pupils in the Greater Manchester and the West Midlands combined authority areas received their GCSE results via an app called Education Record, which automatically collates their key information and exam results.

Across the country, students can access their results on the app from 11am. However, they can still collect their traditional physical results at school starting around 8am.

You can find out more information about the app here.

Forcing teenagers who fail GCSEs into multiple resits has a negative impact on their mental health, according to research to be published as pupils receive their grades on Thursday.

The study by academics at University College London (UCL) compared the mental wellbeing of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland who failed to reach a grade 4 or equivalent in maths or English GCSEs – and found that only those in England, where resits are mandatory, showed significantly lower wellbeing.

Robbie Maris, a research fellow at UCL and one of the authors, said the dent to teenagers’ self-confidence when faced with resits could be a contributing factor to the rise in young people not in education, employment or training, known as Neets.

Maris said: “Some [resitting] students will not turn up for their exams, they won’t enter them or they will drop out of education – these are the kids at highest risk of dropping out of education and becoming Neets.

“It could be leading to further disengagement, which is a worrying thing. People need to pay more attention to this, because if you demotivate or demoralise young people it puts them at risk of dropping out of the education system entirely.”

Good morning and welcome to our GCSE results day live blog.

Today, like every year, hundreds of thousands of pupils across England, Wales and Northern Ireland anxiously await their grades.

In 2025, there was an overall rise in grades among 16-year-olds taking GCSEs and the gap between boys and girls has narrowed to its smallest level since 2016.

Boys showed improved performances in some of the major subjects like maths and English, while girls slipped backwards in their traditionally strong subjects such as English.

The results mean that the gender gap in favour of girls is now the smallest since separate data for 16-year-olds in England was first published in 2016.

Pupils in England who were thought to have been among the worst affected by Covid bounced back in their GCSE results last year, with more achieving top grades despite the disruption of the pandemic.

The percentage of pupils who achieved a grade 7 and above was 23% in 2025, up from 22.6% in 2024. While those who achieved a grade 4 and above (pass) was 70.4%, a slight increase from the previous year.

For pupils in Northern Ireland, the proportion getting A and A* – equivalent to grades 7 and above in England – rose by a full percentage point to 31.4%, while the proportion getting grades C or above went up to 63.8%.

In Wales, where letter grades are also still used, pupils getting the top grades rose to 20.1%, up from 19.8% in 2024, and those getting a C or better edged up by 0.3 percentage points to 63.8%.

If the GCSE results follow last week’s A-level results, it might be a bumper year for grades. The proportion of students in England gaining the highest grade of A* in A-level subjects rose to 9.7%, up from 9.4% last year, setting a new record outside the pandemic era, when exams were scrapped.

Northern Ireland was the best-performing country, with 30.7% of grades being As and A*s, followed by 29.6% in Wales and 28.7% in England.

The GCSE cohort taking exams in 2026 were in Year 5 when the pandemic and subsequent lockdowns began in 2020. They faced severe disruption during key developmental years (perhaps less so than the 2025 cohort, who were in their final year at primary school in 2020), particularly the primary-to-secondary transition period, chronic absenteeism, and mental health challenges.

Follow along as we look at whether the overall 9-4 pass rates are affected in key subjects like English and maths, as well as if girls’ overall results drop again.

articles.title: State-backed Israeli settler violence forces West Bank displacement: HRW
articles.excerpt:
Dozens of Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank are at risk of erasure due to escalating attacks by Israeli settlers, according to a new report by Human Rights Watch.

Increased settler at...
articles.body_text:
Dozens of Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank are at risk of erasure due to escalating attacks by Israeli settlers, according to a new report by Human Rights Watch.

Increased settler attacks, along with the rapid expansion of Israeli settlements illegal under international law, are driving a wave of forced displacement of Palestinians, the US-based rights group said in a report released on Thursday.

The report accuses Israeli authorities of arming, funding and granting impunity to settlers to carry out the attacks.

Israeli settler violence has been growing since the current government took office in December 2022.

But attacks spiked in the first two months of the US and Israel’s war on Iran, with killings including those of children, assaults, sexual violence, physical and mental abuse, arbitrary detention, arson, property demolition and theft among the reported abuses, the report adds.

“The Israeli government and the settlers share the same goal of maximum land and minimum Palestinians, with the authorities not only failing to stop settler violence, but actively enabling it,” Sarah Sanbar, the acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch, said.

“Settlers shoot, attack, and expel Palestinians from their land, and the state provides the weapons, the legal cover, and the budget to do it,” she added.

HRW investigated settler attacks in seven Palestinian West Bank communities in April and May, including Al-Mughayyir, Mikhmas and Taybeh, in Ramallah governorate; Jalud and Qaryut, in Nablus governorate; and Khirbet Hamsa and Muarrajat East, in the Jordan Valley.

The report found that, sometimes, armed settlers acted alongside Israeli military units or with soldiers standing by yet failing to intervene, during raids on Palestinian residents and property, contributing to a pattern of forced displacement.

It said the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) research found more Palestinians were forcibly displaced by settler attacks, demolitions and evictions in the first four months of this year than in the whole of 2025.

OCHA found that 107 communities, comprising 5,900 Palestinians, had been completely or partially displaced as a result of settler violence since January 2023. It also found that the Israeli military expelled another 32,000 Palestinians from their homes in the occupied West Bank since January 2025, essentially emptying the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps.

Human Rights Watch says the attacks and lack of state protection have created a coercive environment that leaves many Palestinians saying they have no choice but to leave their homes.

The report recommended targeted sanctions on those implicated in ongoing abuses, the suspension of weapons transfers to Israel and a trade ban with illegal settlements, and urged countries to consider suspending preferential trade agreements with Israel.

“The impunity Israeli authorities accord settlers stems directly from the free pass Israel’s allies and donors have granted it,” Sanbar said.

“Israel and the governments that give it a blank check share responsibility and should be held to account,” she said.

articles.title: Sales of trainers dive as cost of living pressures hit JD Sports performance
articles.excerpt:
Inflation deterring shoppers from spending, especially in the US, says sportswear fashion chain

Sports fashion retailer JD has slashed its profit forecasts as cost-of-living pressures, fuelled by the...
articles.body_text:
Inflation deterring shoppers from spending, especially in the US, says sportswear fashion chain

Sports fashion retailer JD has slashed its profit forecasts as cost-of-living pressures, fuelled by the US war on Iran, weighed on sales of trainers.

JD Sports, which sells a range of sports brands including Nike and Adidas, said widespread inflation had hit shoppers’ wallets, resulting in falling sales across important markets such as the US, where it struggled to quickly shift trainers and other footwear.

Bosses went on to warn that the wider drop-off in consumer spending would likely continue into the second half of the year, leading to lower-than-expected profits. The sports retailer now expects pre-tax profits of between £700m and £800m for the full year, having previously hoped to reach £750m to £850m.

The news led to a 12% drop in the firm’s London-listed shares, falling on Thursday morning to their lowest level since July.

“Trading in the second quarter remained tough,” the chief executive, Régis Schultz, adding that the company had been forced to slash prices and offer promotional sales to compensate, as “our core consumer was impacted by incremental cost-of-living pressures.”

The company, which runs 4,800 stores worldwide including the JD, Blacks and Millets chains in the UK, said pressures included higher fuel prices, which have been pushed up by the US-Israeli war on Iran which has effectively stopped tanker traffic through the strait of Hormuz.

Overall, JD said its like-for-like sales fell by 3.1% in the second quarter, with its North America operations taking the biggest hit, falling by 6.8%. Sales across Europe tumbled by 2.7% during the same period.

The UK was a rare bright spot, as World Cup excitement drove sales of football replica kits, while consumers bought more outdoor gear, including from its high street brands Blacks and Go Outdoors.

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist, at investment firm Wealth Club said: “JD Sports is offering another glimpse of the darkening clouds gathering over the US economy, with American shoppers looking considerably more cautious.

“The sneaker is fast becoming a canary in the coal mine for confidence,” she said. “More consumers are resisting the lure of hyped brands, which is not surprising when the jobs market is weakening and inflation is still such a concern. Consumers may still be spending, but they are becoming more selective about discretionary purchases, particularly when household budgets are already under pressure.”
